rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is called al-Fatiha because it opens the written Book and begins recitation in prayer.
rows.anchor: أي : فاتحة الكتاب خطا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority call it Umm al-Kitab; Anas is cited for this name.
rows.anchor: ويقال لها أيضا : أم الكتاب عند الجمهور ، ذكره أنس

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن سيرين
rows.claim: Hasan and Ibn Sirin dislike the name Umm al-Kitab, taking it to refer to the Preserved Tablet; Hasan also calls the clear verses Umm al-Kitab.
rows.anchor: والحسن وابن سيرين كرها تسميتها بذلك ، قال الحسن وابن سيرين : إنما ذلك اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan also objects to calling the surah Umm al-Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن : الآيات المحكمات : هن أم الكتاب

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In a hadith graded sound by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet calls it Umm al-Qur'an, Umm al-Kitab, the seven oft-repeated, and the great Qur'an.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : «الحمد لله أم القرآن وأم الكتاب والسبع المثاني والقرآن العظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hamd is another name for the surah.
rows.anchor: ويقال لها : الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is also called al-Salah because the divine hadith names recitation of al-Hamd as the servant's praise, and the surah is a condition of prayer.
rows.anchor: فسميت الفاتحة : صلاة ؛ لأنها شرط فيها

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Abu Saʿid calls the Fatiha a healing from every poison.
rows.anchor: فاتحة الكتاب شفاء من كل سم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The surah is called a ruqya because the Prophet affirmed its use in healing a stung man and asked how the companion knew it was a ruqya.
rows.anchor: فقال له رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : «وما يدريك أنها رقية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas calls the surah the foundation of the Qur'an and says its foundation is the basmala.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه سماها : أساس القرآن

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna calls the surah al-Waqiya, the protecting one.
rows.anchor: وسماها سفيان بن عيينة : الواقية

rows.speaker: يحيى بن أبي كثير
rows.claim: Yahya ibn Abi Kathir calls it al-Kafiya: it suffices in place of other surahs, while none can replace it; this is also stated in a mursal report.
rows.anchor: وسماها يحيى بن أبي كثير : الكافية ؛ لأنها تكفي عما عداها ولا يكفي ما سواها عنها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari also records the names Surat al-Salah and al-Kanz.
rows.anchor: ويقال لها : سورة الصلاة والكنز ذكرهما الزمخشري

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة وأبو العالية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, and Abu al-ʿAliya hold that the surah was revealed in Mecca.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس وقتادة وأبو العالية

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة ومجاهد وعطاء بن يسار والزهري
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra, Mujahid, ʿAta ibn Yasar, and al-Zuhri hold that the surah was revealed in Medina.
rows.anchor: أبو هريرة ومجاهد وعطاء بن يسار والزهري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third report says it was revealed twice, but Ibn Kathir prefers the Meccan account, connecting it with the seven oft-repeated in 15:87.
rows.anchor: ومرة بالمدينة ،   والأول أشبه

rows.speaker: أبو الليث السمرقندي
rows.claim: Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi says half the surah was revealed in Mecca and half in Medina; Ibn Kathir calls this very strange, as transmitted by al-Qurtubi.
rows.anchor: وحكى أبو الليث السمرقندي أن نصفها نزل بمكة ونصفها الآخر نزل بالمدينة ، وهو غريب جدًا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no disagreement that the surah has seven verses; reports of eight from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd and six from Husayn al-Juʿfi are aberrant.
rows.anchor: وهي سبع آيات بلا خلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars differ over whether the basmala is an independent opening verse, part of a verse, or not counted as part of the Fatiha.
rows.anchor: هل هي آية مستقلة من أولها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah has twenty-five words and one hundred thirteen letters.
rows.anchor: كلماتها خمس وعشرون كلمة ، وحروفها مائة وثلاثة عشر حرفًا

rows.speaker: البخاري
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari explains Umm al-Kutub by its being written first in Qur'anic codices and recited first in prayer.
rows.anchor: وسميت أم الكتب ، أنه يبدأ بكتابتها في المصاحف ، ويبدأ بقراءتها في الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation of Umm al-Kitab is that the meanings of the whole Qur'an return to what the Fatiha contains.
rows.anchor: سميت بذلك لرجوع معاني القرآن كله

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir says Arabs call a comprehensive or leading thing with dependent parts an umm, such as the head's covering or an army's banner.
rows.anchor: والعرب تسمي كل جامع أمر

rows.speaker: ذو الرمة
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir cites Dhu al-Rumma's verse calling a spear an umm, a focal point followed in affairs.
rows.anchor: على رأسه أم لنا نقتدي به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mecca is called Umm al-Qura because it precedes and gathers the other settlements, or because the earth was spread from it.
rows.anchor: وسميت مكة : أم القرى لتقدمها أمام جميعها وجمعها ما سواها ، وقيل : لأن الأرض دحيت منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Fatiha opens recitation and was placed first when the Companions wrote the master codex.
rows.anchor: ويقال لها أيضًا : الفاتحة ؛ لأنها تفتتح بها القراءة ، وافتتحت الصحابة بها كتابة المصحف الإمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title al-Sabʿ al-Mathani is explained by its repetition in every prayer unit, though Ibn Kathir notes another meaning will follow.
rows.anchor: قالوا : لأنها تثنى في الصلاة ، فتقرأ في كل ركعة ، وإن كان للمثاني معنى آخر

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Reports from Abu Hurayra identify Umm al-Qur'an as the Fatiha and the seven oft-repeated; al-Daraqutni says its transmitters are trustworthy.
rows.anchor: هي أم القرآن ، وهي فاتحة الكتاب ، وهي السبع المثاني

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس وأبو هريرة
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi reports that ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu Hurayra interpret the seven oft-repeated in 15:87 as the Fatiha, with the basmala its seventh verse.
rows.anchor: وروى البيهقي عن علي{[31]} وابن عباس{[32]} وأبي هريرة{[33]} أنهم

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud explains that he omitted the Fatiha from his codex because he would have written it at the start of every surah where it is recited in prayer; Muslims' memorization sufficed.
rows.anchor: لو كتبتها لكتبتها في أول كل سورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes the Fatiha the first revelation, based on a report in al-Bayhaqi and listed by al-Baqillani among three views.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل : إن الفاتحة أول شيء نزل من القرآن ، كما ورد في حديث رواه البيهقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view makes “O you wrapped up” the first revelation, based on Jabir's sound hadith.
rows.anchor: وقيل : { يَا أَيُّهَا الْمُدَّثِّرُ } كما في حديث جابر في الصحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says the correct view is that “Read in the name of your Lord” was first revealed.
rows.anchor: وقيل : { اقْرَأْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ } [ العلق : 1 ] وهذا هو الصحيح

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla reports that the Prophet promised to teach him the Qur'an's greatest surah and identified it as al-Hamd, the seven oft-repeated and the great Qur'an.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله رب العالمين هي : السبع المثاني والقرآن العظيم الذي أوتيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir distinguishes the Muwatta's Abu Saʿid, a Successor and client of Khuzāʿa, from the Companion Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla; the former report appears disconnected unless he heard it from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.
rows.anchor: فأبو سعيد هذا ليس بأبي سعيد بن المعلى ، كما اعتقده ابن الأثير

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report through Abu Hurayra from Ubayy repeats that the Fatiha has no equal in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an; al-Tirmidhi calls it hasan sahih.
rows.anchor: إني لأرجو ألا أخرج من هذا الباب حتى تعلمها

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Another report from Ubayy calls Umm al-Qur'an the seven oft-repeated, divided between God and His servant; al-Tirmidhi grades it hasan gharib.
rows.anchor: ما أنزل الله في التوراة ولا في الإنجيل مثل أم القرآن ، وهي السبع المثاني ، وهي مقسومة بيني وبين عبدي

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن جابر
rows.claim: The report that the Prophet called the Fatiha the best surah has a good chain according to Ibn Kathir; the Companion's identity is uncertain between al-ʿAbdi and al-Ansari al-Bayyadi.
rows.anchor: هذا إسناد جيد ،   وابن عقيل تحتج{[60]} به الأئمة الكبار ،   وعبد الله بن جابر هذا هو الصحابي

rows.speaker: إسحاق بن راهويه وأبو بكر بن العربي وابن الحصار
rows.claim: These scholars infer that some verses and surahs are superior to others from the superiority reports.
rows.anchor: واستدلوا بهذا الحديث وأمثاله على تفاضل بعض الآيات والسور

rows.speaker: الأشعري وأبو بكر الباقلاني وابن حبان ويحيى بن يحيى
rows.claim: Another group denies ranking Qur'anic passages, since all are God's speech and ranking could imply deficiency in what is less preferred; a report from Malik agrees.
rows.anchor: وذهبت طائفة أخرى إلى أنه لا تفاضل في ذلك ؛ لأن الجميع كلام الله ، ولئلا يوهم التفضيل نقص المفضل عليه

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: In a report judged by the Prophet, a companion recited the Fatiha as ruqya over a stung man who recovered; the Prophet approved the reward of thirty sheep and asked how he knew it was ruqya.
rows.anchor: فبرأ ، فأمر له بثلاثين شاة ، وسقانا لبنا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that Gabriel announced two lights given to Muhammad alone: the Fatiha and the closing verses of al-Baqara; each letter brings a response.
rows.anchor: أبشر بنورين قد أوتيتهما لم يؤتهما نبي قبلك : فاتحة الكتاب ، وخواتيم سورة البقرة

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says prayer without Umm al-Qur'an is deficient, and the divine hadith answers the servant's praise verse by verse as the Fatiha is divided between God and servant.
rows.anchor: فهي خِداج - ثلاثًا - غير تمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the divine hadith, “prayer” means recitation, as in 17:110; because the Fatiha details the division, its recitation is a major pillar of prayer.
rows.anchor: أي : بقراءتك كما جاء مصرحًا به في الصحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Qur'an of dawn” in 17:78 means the dawn prayer, as the sound reports say angels of night and day witness it; scholars agree prayer requires recitation.
rows.anchor: والمراد صلاة الفجر ، كما جاء مصرحا به في الصحيحين

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأصحابه
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and his followers hold that Fatiha is not specifically required in prayer; any Qur'an passage suffices, citing 73:20 and “recite what is easy.”
rows.anchor: فعند أبي حنيفة ومن وافقه من أصحابه وغيرهم أنها لا تتعين

rows.speaker: مالك والشافعي وأحمد والجمهور
rows.claim: The other major view requires the Fatiha in prayer, using the deficient-prayer hadith and reports that prayer does not count without it.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : أنه تتعين قراءة الفاتحة في الصلاة ، ولا تجزئ الصلاة بدونها

rows.speaker: الشافعي وجماعة من أهل العلم
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi and a group require the Fatiha in every prayer unit; others require it in most units, while Hasan and most Basrans require it in one unit.
rows.anchor: أنه تجب قراءتها في كل ركعة

rows.speaker: الحسن وأكثر البصريين
rows.claim: Hasan and most Basrans require the Fatiha in only one unit, relying on the unrestricted wording, “There is no prayer without Fatiha.”
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وأكثر البصريين : إنما تجب قراءتها في ركعة واحدة من الصلوات

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة والثوري والأوزاعي
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, and al-Awzaʿi again hold that another Qur'anic passage can replace the Fatiha, citing 73:20.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة وأصحابه والثوري والأوزاعي : لا تتعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report that each prayer unit needs al-Hamd and another surah is questionable in authenticity.
rows.anchor: وفي صحة هذا نظر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars have three views on whether a follower must recite: that the follower must recite the Fatiha just like the imam.
rows.anchor: أحدها : أنه تجب عليه قراءتها ، كما تجب على إمامه

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: A second view says a follower recites nothing, whether prayer is audible or silent, based on “one with an imam has the imam's recitation”; the marfuʿ routes are weak, and Malik transmits it as Jabir's own statement.
rows.anchor: من كان له إمام فقراءة الإمام له قراءة » ولكن في إسناده ضعف

rows.speaker: الشافعي في قوله القديم وأحمد في رواية
rows.claim: A third view requires the follower's recitation in silent prayer but not audible prayer, combining the general requirement with the command to listen when the imam recites.
rows.anchor: أنه تجب القراءة على المأموم في السرية

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Al-Bazzar reports that reciting the Fatiha and Surat al-Ikhlas before sleep protects from everything except death.
rows.anchor: فقد أمنت من كل شيء إلا الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Three Qur'anic passages distinguish how to handle human and satanic enemies: kindness can turn a human enemy into a friend, while Satan must be met with refuge in God.
rows.anchor: وهو أن الله يأمر بمصانعة العدو الإنسي والإحسان إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan seeks Adam's descendants' ruin because of his inherited enmity, having already deceived their parents and sworn to mislead all but God's sincere servants.
rows.anchor: إذ لا يقبل مصانعة ولا إحسانا ولا يبتغي غير هلاك ابن آدم

rows.speaker: حمزة وأبو حاتم السجستاني
rows.claim: Some readers place istiʿadha after recitation, taking 16:98 literally and to ward off self-admiration after worship; Ibn Kathir attributes this view to Hamza and Abu Hatim.
rows.anchor: قالت طائفة من القراء وغيرهم : نتعوذ بعد القراءة ، واعتمدوا على ظاهر سياق الآية

rows.speaker: ابن سيرين وإبراهيم النخعي وداود بن علي
rows.claim: Ibn Sirin in one report, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, and Dawud al-Zahiri are also said to place istiʿadha after recitation.
rows.anchor: عن ابن سيرين في رواية عنه قال : وهو قول إبراهيم النخعي وداود بن علي

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: A report attributed to Malik also places istiʿadha after the Fatiha; Ibn al-ʿArabi regards it as strange.
rows.anchor: أن القارئ يتعوذ بعد الفاتحة ، واستغربه ابن العربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third position combines both reports by seeking refuge both before and after recitation.
rows.anchor: وحكي قول ثالث وهو الاستعاذة أولا وآخرا جمعا بين الدليلين

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The well-known majority view is to seek refuge before recitation to repel satanic whispering; “when you read” means when you intend to read, as in 5:6.
rows.anchor: والمشهور الذي عليه الجمهور أن الاستعاذة لدفع الوسواس فيها ، إنما تكون قبل التلاوة

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Saʿid al-Khudri reports that the Prophet began night prayer with praise and then sought refuge from the devil's hamz, nafkh, and nafth; al-Tirmidhi calls it the best-known report in this topic.
rows.anchor: أعوذ بالله السميع العليم ، من الشيطان الرجيم ، من همزه ونفخه ونفثه

rows.speaker: عمرو بن مرة
rows.claim: The terms are explained as hamz meaning seizure or suffocation, nafkh meaning pride, and nafth meaning poetry.
rows.anchor: وهمزه الموتة ، ونفخه الكبر ، ونفثه الشعر

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Jubayr ibn Mutʿim gives the same refuge formula at the start of prayer and explains hamz, nafkh, and nafth in the same way.
rows.anchor: اللهم إني أعوذ بك من الشيطان من همزه ونفخه ونفثه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud reports the Prophet taught the prayer: “I seek refuge in You from the accursed Satan, his hamz, nafkh, and nafth,” with the terms explained as seizure, pride, and poetry.
rows.anchor: اللهم إني أعوذ بك من الشيطان الرجيم ، وهمزه ونفخه ونفثه

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة الباهلي
rows.claim: Abu Umama reports that the Prophet used the refuge formula after repeated takbirs and praises when beginning prayer.
rows.anchor: أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم ، من همزه ونفخه ونفثه

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb reports that when a man became enraged during a dispute, the Prophet said a formula of seeking refuge would remove his anger.
rows.anchor: إني لأعلم شيئا لو قاله ذهب عنه ما يجد : أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: A parallel report through Muʿadh says the same formula would end a man's anger; al-Tirmidhi calls it mursal because Ibn Abi Layla did not meet Muʿadh.
rows.anchor: وقال الترمذي : مرسل ، يعني أن عبد الرحمن بن أبي ليلى لم يلق معاذ بن جبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir suggests Ibn Abi Layla may have heard the story from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and says several Companions witnessed it.
rows.anchor: وقد يكون عبد الرحمن بن أبي ليلى سمعه من أبي بن كعب ، كما تقدم

rows.speaker: سليمان بن صرد
rows.claim: Sulayman ibn Surad reports that the Prophet advised an angry, red-faced man to say “I seek refuge in God from Satan”; the man dismissed the advice, saying he was not mad.
rows.anchor: إني لأعلم كلمة لو قالها لذهب عنه ما يجد ، لو قال : أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says Gabriel first taught Muhammad to seek refuge, then the basmala, then Surat al-ʿAlaq; Ibn Kathir calls it strange, weak in chain, and disconnected.
rows.anchor: أول ما نزل جبريل على محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : يا محمد ، استعذ

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most scholars regard istiʿadha as recommended rather than obligatory.
rows.anchor: وجمهور العلماء على أن الاستعاذة مستحبة ليست بمتحتمة

rows.speaker: عطاء بن أبي رباح
rows.claim: ʿAta ibn Abi Rabah holds that istiʿadha is obligatory in and outside prayer whenever one intends to recite.
rows.anchor: وحكى فخر الدين عن عطاء بن أبي رباح وجوبها في الصلاة وخارجها كلما أراد القراءة

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi argues for ʿAta's obligation view from the imperative wording, the Prophet's regular practice, its protection from Satan, and the rule that a necessary means to a duty is itself required.
rows.anchor: وهو أمر ظاهره الوجوب وبمواظبة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عليها

rows.speaker: ابن سيرين
rows.claim: Ibn Sirin is also reported to say that a single istiʿadha in one's lifetime suffices to discharge the obligation.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن سيرين : إذا تعوذ مرة واحدة في عمره فقد كفى في إسقاط الوجوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say istiʿadha was obligatory for the Prophet alone; Malik is reported not to use it in obligatory prayers but to use it on the first night of Ramadan's night prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : كانت واجبة على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم دون أمته

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi says in al-Imlaʾ that istiʿadha is recited aloud though silence is harmless; in al-Umm he gives the choice, citing Ibn ʿUmar's silence and Abu Hurayra's loud recitation.
rows.anchor: وقال الشافعي في الإملاء ، يجهر بالتعوذ ، وإن أسر فلا يضر

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi had two views on repeating istiʿadha in later prayer units and preferred that it not be repeated.
rows.anchor: واختلف قول الشافعي فيما عدا الركعة الأولى : هل يستحب التعوذ فيها ؟ على قولين ، ورجح عدم الاستحباب

rows.speaker: الشافعي وأبو حنيفة
rows.claim: For al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifa, “I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed” is sufficient; some add “the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.”
rows.anchor: فإذا قال المستعيذ : أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم كفى ذلك عند الشافعي وأبي حنيفة

rows.speaker: الثوري والأوزاعي
rows.claim: Al-Thawri and al-Awzaʿi add “God is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing” to the refuge formula, while another group prefers “I seek refuge” to match the Qur'anic wording; Ibn Kathir prefers sound hadith.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون : بل يقول : أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم إن الله هو السميع العليم

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة ومحمد وأبو يوسف
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and Muhammad say istiʿadha in prayer is for recitation; Abu Yusuf says it is for prayer itself, so his view requires a nonreciting follower to say it and places it before Eid takbirs.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو يوسف : بل للصلاة ، فعلى هذا يتعوذ المأموم وإن كان لا يقرأ

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority say istiʿadha at Eid follows the opening takbir and precedes recitation.
rows.anchor: والجمهور بعدها قبل القراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istiʿadha cleans and prepares the mouth for recitation, seeks God's aid, and admits human weakness against an inward enemy whom only God can repel.
rows.anchor: ومن لطائف الاستعاذة أنها طهارة للفم مما كان يتعاطاه من اللغو والرفث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istiʿadha means seeking shelter with God from harm to one's religion or worldly life, diversion from commands, and temptation toward prohibitions.
rows.anchor: ومعنى أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم ، أي : أستجير بجناب الله من الشيطان الرجيم أن يضرني في ديني أو دنياي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking refuge repels harm, while seeking shelter or attachment (liyadh) asks for good; Ibn Kathir illustrates the distinction with al-Mutanabbi's poem.
rows.anchor: والعياذة تكون لدفع الشر ، واللياذ يكون لطلب جلب الخير

rows.speaker: المتنبي
rows.claim: Al-Mutanabbi's cited poem contrasts taking refuge from what one fears with seeking shelter in the one from whom one hopes aid.
rows.anchor: يا من ألوذ به فيما أؤمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans can see Satan while Satan sees humans; refuge is sought from the One who sees Satan and cannot be seen by him.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الشيطان يرى الإنسان من حيث لا يراه استعاذ منه بالذي يراه ولا يراه الشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human adversary may be repelled by kindness, but the jinn adversary accepts neither bribery nor good treatment and can only be checked by God.
rows.anchor: وأمر بالاستعاذة به من شيطان الجن لأنه لا يقبل رشوة ولا يؤثر فيه جميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inward enemy's victory leaves one tempted or burdened by sin; defeating the visible enemy earns reward, while those slain by human enemies are martyrs.
rows.anchor: ومن قتله العدو البشري كان شهيدًا ، ومن قتله العدو الباطني كان طريدًا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says angels came to fight the human enemy at Badr.
rows.anchor: وقد نزلت الملائكة لمقاتلة العدو البشري يوم بدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istiʿadha is a plea for refuge and clinging to God's protection from every source of harm.
rows.anchor: والاستعاذة هي الالتجاء إلى الله والالتصاق بجنابه من شر كل ذي شر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God instructs people to treat a human devil with good conduct, but to seek refuge from the jinn devil because it cannot be softened by kindness.
rows.anchor: فإن الشيطان لا يكفه عن الإنسان إلا الله ؛ ولهذا أمر الله تعالى بمصانعة شيطان الإنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir prefers deriving shaytan from shatana, “to be distant”; the alternative links it to shata, “to burn,” since Satan was created from fire, and both fit the sense.
rows.anchor: وقيل : مشتق من شاط لأنه مخلوق من نار ، ومنهم من يقول : كلاهما صحيح في المعنى ، ولكن الأول أصح

rows.speaker: أمية بن أبي الصلت
rows.claim: Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's verse says shatin, not shait, supporting derivation from distance rather than burning.
rows.anchor: أيما شاطِنٍ عصاه عكاه *** ثمّ يُلْقى في السِّجْن

rows.speaker: النابغة الذبياني
rows.claim: Al-Nabigha's poem uses shatun for a far-off journey, evidence for shaytan's derivation from distance.
rows.anchor: نأت بسعاد عنك نوى شطون

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh notes Arabs say “tashaytan” for acting like a devil; if derived from shata, they would say “tashayyat.”
rows.anchor: العرب تقول : تشيطن فلان إذا فعل فعل الشيطان ولو كان من شاط لقالوا : تشيط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Shaytan” can name any rebellious jinn, human, or animal, as in 6:112; Abu Dharr's report confirms that humans too have devils.
rows.anchor: من جني وإنسي وحيوان شيطانًا

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Dharr asked whether humans have devils too, and the Prophet replied yes.
rows.anchor: يا أبا ذر ، تعوذ بالله من شياطين الإنس والجن

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In a report about prayer being interrupted by a woman, donkey, or black dog, the Prophet calls the black dog a devil.
rows.anchor: الكلب الأسود شيطان

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: A report with a sound chain says ʿUmar dismounted an unruly prancing horse and called it a devil because it altered his disposition.
rows.anchor: عن زيد بن أسلم ،   عن أبيه ،   أن عمر بن الخطاب ،   رضي الله عنه ،   ركب برْذونًا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajim is the passive sense of faʿil: Satan is pelted and expelled from all good, as in verses about shooting stars driving devils away.
rows.anchor: والرجيم : فعيل بمعنى مفعول ، أي : إنه مرجوم مطرود عن الخير كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A less common interpretation makes rajim active, “one who pelts” people with whispers and corruptions; Ibn Kathir says the passive interpretation is better known.
rows.anchor: وقيل : رجيم بمعنى راجم ؛ لأنه يرجم الناس بالوساوس والربائث والأول أشهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Companions opened God's Book with the basmala; scholars agree it is part of the verse in Surat al-Naml, while disputing its status at surah openings.
rows.anchor: افتتح بها الصحابة كتاب الله ، واتفق العلماء على أنها بعض آية من سورة النمل

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A sound Abu Dawud report from Ibn ʿAbbas says the Prophet recognized a surah's division when the basmala was revealed; it is also reported mursal from Saʿid ibn Jubayr.
rows.anchor: كان لا يعرف فصل السورة حتى ينزل عليه

rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet recited and counted the basmala as a verse at the start of the Fatiha; Ibn Kathir notes the chain is weak because of ʿUmar ibn Harun.
rows.anchor: عن أم سلمة : أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قرأ البسملة في أول الفاتحة في الصلاة وعدّها آية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن عمر وابن الزبير وأبو هريرة وعلي
rows.claim: These Companions are cited as holding that the basmala is a verse at the start of every surah except al-Tawba; several Successors and a group of later authorities agree.
rows.anchor: وممن حكي عنه أنها آية من كل سورة إلا براءة : ابن عباس ، وابن عمر ، وابن الزبير

rows.speaker: مالك وأبو حنيفة وأصحابهما
rows.claim: Malik, Abu Hanifa, and their followers say the basmala is not a verse of the Fatiha or any other surah.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك وأبو حنيفة وأصحابهما : ليست آية من الفاتحة ولا من غيرها من السور

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: One Shafiʿi position makes the basmala a verse of the Fatiha alone; another makes it part of the first verse of every surah, and Ibn Kathir calls both views unusual.
rows.anchor: وقال الشافعي في قول ، في بعض طرق مذهبه : هي آية من الفاتحة وليست من غيرها

rows.speaker: داود وأحمد
rows.claim: Dawud and one narration from Ahmad treat the basmala as an independent opening verse of each surah, not part of the surahs.
rows.anchor: وقال داود : هي آية مستقلة في أول كل سورة لا منها

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi recites the basmala aloud with both Fatiha and the following surah when opening prayer; many early and later authorities also did so.
rows.anchor: فذهب الشافعي ، رحمه الله ، إلى أنه يجهر بها مع الفاتحة والسورة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra recited the basmala aloud and said his prayer most resembled the Prophet's; Ibn Kathir cites several scholars who authenticated the report.
rows.anchor: أنه صلى فجهر في قراءته بالبسملة ، وقال بعد أن فرغ : إني لأشبهكم صلاة برسول الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that the Prophet opened prayer with the basmala; al-Tirmidhi says its chain is not strong.
rows.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يفتتح الصلاة ببسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas describes the Prophet's recitation as prolonged, with lengthening on each word of the basmala.
rows.anchor: كانت قراءته مدا ، ثم قرأ بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم ، يمد بسم الله

rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: Umm Salama says the Prophet paused phrase by phrase in recitation, and al-Daraqutni calls the report's chain sound.
rows.anchor: عن أم سلمة ، قالت{[812]} : كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقطع قراءته

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: When Muʿawiya omitted the basmala in Medina, the Muhajirun present objected; on his next prayer he recited it.
rows.anchor: فترك البسملة ، فأنكر عليه من حضره من المهاجرين ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة والثوري وأحمد
rows.claim: Another group does not recite the basmala aloud; Ibn Kathir says this is established from the four caliphs, Ibn Mughaffal, and other early authorities.
rows.anchor: وذهب آخرون إلى أنه لا يجهر بالبسملة في الصلاة ، وهذا هو الثابت عن الخلفاء الأربعة

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik does not recite the basmala in prayer either aloud or quietly, relying on reports that the Prophet and first caliphs began with al-Hamd and did not mention it.
rows.anchor: وعند الإمام مالك : أنه لا يقرأ البسملة بالكلية ، لا جهرًا ولا سرًّا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The legal disagreement is narrow: scholars agree a prayer is valid whether the basmala is recited aloud or quietly.
rows.anchor: لأنهم أجمعوا على صحة صلاة من جهر بالبسملة ومن أسر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says the basmala is one of God's names, extremely close to the Greatest Name, like the closeness between the black and white of the eye.
rows.anchor: هو اسم من أسماء الله ، وما بينه وبين اسم الله الأكبر ، إلا كما بين سواد العينين وبياضهما

rows.speaker: عيسى ابن مريم
rows.claim: A report explains the letters as bāʾ for God's splendor, sīn for His glory, and mīm for His dominion; Rahman is merciful in both worlds and Rahim in the next. Ibn Kathir calls the report very strange and possibly Israelite rather than Prophetic.
rows.anchor: الباء بهاء الله ، والسين سناؤه ، والميم مملكته

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak is said to have transmitted a similar explanation of the basmala.
rows.anchor: وقد روى جُوَيبر{[824]} ، عن الضحَّاك ،   نحوه من قبله

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Burayda says the basmala was revealed to Muhammad and Solomon alone.
rows.anchor: أنزلت علي آية لم تنزل على نبي غير سليمان بن داود وغيري ، وهي بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jabir's report describes clouds fleeing, winds and sea becoming still, animals listening, devils pelted, and God's promise of blessing when His name is said over something.
rows.anchor: عن جابر بن عبد الله ،   قال : لما نزل

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud reportedly says reciting the basmala shields a person from each of the nineteen keepers of Hell; Ibn ʿAtiyya supports this with a report of more than thirty angels hastening to record praise.
rows.anchor: من أراد أن ينجيه الله من الزبانية التسعة عشر فليقرأ : بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says not to curse Satan after a fall because that makes him swell with pride; saying “in God's name” makes him shrink like a fly (another version says like a house).
rows.anchor: لا تقل تعس الشيطان . فإنك إذا قلت : تعس الشيطان تعاظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the basmala humbles Satan, it is recommended at the beginning of actions and speech.
rows.anchor: فهذا من تأثير بركة بسم الله ؛ ولهذا تستحب في أوّل كل عمل وقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report recommends beginning a sermon with the basmala and calls an affair begun without it defective.
rows.anchor: لا يبدأ فيه ببسم الله الرحمن الرحيم ،   فهو أجذم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basmala is recommended on entering the toilet, based on reports transmitted on that practice.
rows.anchor: وتستحب البسملة عند دخول الخلاء ولما ورد من الحديث في ذلك

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A hadith judged hasan says there is no ablution for one who does not mention God's name; scholars differ over whether it is obligatory when remembered or absolutely.
rows.anchor: من رواية أبي هريرة ،   وسعيد بن زيد ،   وأبي سعيد مرفوعًا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basmala is recommended before slaughter according to al-Shafiʿi and a group; others require it if remembered, and some require it absolutely.
rows.anchor: وكذا تستحب عند الذبيحة في مذهب الشافعي وجماعة ، وأوجبها آخرون عند الذكر

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet instructed his stepson ʿUmar ibn Abi Salama to say God's name, eat with his right hand, and eat from what is nearest; some scholars make the basmala obligatory at meals.
rows.anchor: قل : باسم الله ، وكل بيمينك ، وكل مما يليك

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet taught spouses to say God's name and ask protection from Satan before intercourse; if a child is conceived, Satan will not harm it.
rows.anchor: لو أن أحدكم إذا أتى أهله قال : باسم الله ، اللهم جنبنا الشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition bi in the basmala may attach to an implied noun, “my beginning,” or verb, “I begin”; Qur'anic usage supports both.
rows.anchor: هل هو اسم أو فعل متقاربان وكل قد ورد به القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied action varies with the activity begun—standing, sitting, eating, drinking, reciting, ablution, or prayer—and the basmala seeks blessing, aid to completion, and acceptance.
rows.anchor: وذلك بحسب الفعل الذي سميت قبله ، إن كان قيامًا أو قعودًا أو أكلا أو شربًا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In a report on the first revelation, Gabriel tells Muhammad to say the basmala and explains it as beginning, standing, and sitting in remembrance of God; Ibn Kathir elsewhere calls the report weak and disconnected.
rows.anchor: قال له جبريل : قل : باسم الله يا محمد ، يقول : اقرأ بذكر الله ربك

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة وسيبويه
rows.claim: One position identifies a name with the named object; Abu ʿUbayda and Sibawayh hold this view, as do al-Baqillani and Ibn Furak.
rows.anchor: أن الاسم هو المسمى ، وهو قول أبي عبيدة وسيبويه

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi reports that the Hashwiyya, Karramiyya, and Ashʿariyya identify name and named but distinguish both from naming, while the Muʿtazila distinguish name from named and equate it with naming; he chooses a third view.
rows.anchor: قالت الحشوية والكرامية والأشعرية : الاسم نفس المسمى وغير التسمية ، وقالت المعتزلة : الاسم غير المسمى ونفس التسمية

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi's preferred view is that the name differs from both the named thing and the act of naming.
rows.anchor: والمختار عندنا : أن الاسم غير المسمى وغير التسمية

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi argues that names can exist without their referents, one thing can have many names, one name can refer to many things, and a word is an accident while its referent may be an entity.
rows.anchor: قد يكون الاسم موجودًا والمسمى مفقودًا كلفظة المعدوم

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says God's many names refer to one God and that calling God by those names indicates their distinction from Him.
rows.anchor: فهذه أسماء كثيرة والمسمى واحد وهو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Those who equate name and named cite “blessed is the name of your Lord”; al-Razi answers that honoring the name honors the sacred essence, and a divorce utterance refers to the person bearing that name.
rows.anchor: والجواب : أن الاسم معظم لتعظيم الذات المقدسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah is the proper name of the Lord and is called the Greatest Name because all the other attributes are predicated of Him.
rows.anchor: على الرب تبارك وتعالى ، يقال : إنه الاسم الأعظم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A sound hadith says God has ninety-nine names; whoever comprehends them enters Paradise, though the enumerated lists in al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah differ.
rows.anchor: إن لله تسعة وتسعين اسما ، مائة إلا واحدًا من أحصاها دخل الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah is a name not used for anyone else, and Arabic does not clearly derive it from an ordinary verb.
rows.anchor: وهو اسم لم يسم به غيره تبارك وتعالى ؛ ولهذا لا يعرف في كلام العرب له اشتقاق من فعل ويفعل

rows.speaker: الشافعي والخطابي وإمام الحرمين والغزالي والخليل وسيبويه
rows.claim: These scholars regard Allah as an underived, fixed proper name; al-Khattabi argues that the vocative “ya Allah” works, whereas “ya al-Rahman” does not.
rows.anchor: فذهب من ذهب من النحاة إلى أنه اسم جامد لا اشتقاق له

rows.speaker: رؤبة بن العجاج
rows.claim: Ruʾba's line uses taʾalluh, worship, as evidence that Allah is derived from the root for worship.
rows.anchor: سبحن واسترجعن من تألهي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas's reading “wa-yadharuka wa-ilahatak” is explained as “your worship”; Mujahid gives the same gloss.
rows.anchor: كما روي أن ابن عباس قرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who derive Allah from divinity cite that God is worshipped in heaven and earth and is a god in both realms.
rows.anchor: أي : المعبود في السماوات والأرض

rows.speaker: الخليل وسيبويه
rows.claim: Al-Khalil and Sibawayh derive the word from ilah, with the article replacing an initial hamza, by analogy with al-nas from unas; another proposal takes it from lah for exalted.
rows.anchor: أن أصله : إلاه ، مثل فعال ، فأدخلت الألف واللام بدلا من الهمزة

rows.speaker: الكسائي والفراء
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi and al-Farraʾ derive it from al-ilah, with the hamza dropped and the two lams assimilated, like lakinna from lakin ana.
rows.anchor: أصله : الإله حذفوا الهمزة وأدغموا اللام الأولى في الثانية

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi lists proposed derivations from bewilderment, repose in God, concealment, a calf's attachment to its mother, and seeking refuge in God.
rows.anchor: ثم قيل : هو مشتق من وله : إذا تحير

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says God alone is the refuge and provider, citing that He protects and cannot be protected against, gives every blessing, feeds without being fed, and all things come from Him.
rows.anchor: فالمجير لجميع الخلائق من كل المضار هو الله سبحانه

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi chooses Allah as an underived proper name; he argues that if it were derived, others could share its meaning, while the other names function as attributes.
rows.anchor: وقد اختار فخر الدين أنه اسم علم غير مشتق البتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi also cites 19:65, “Do you know anyone like Him?” as evidence for an un-derived name, but Ibn Kathir finds that argument debatable.
rows.anchor: وفي الاستدلال بهذه على كون هذا الاسم جامدًا غير مشتق نظر

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi rejects the claim that the name Allah is Hebrew rather than Arabic.
rows.anchor: وحكى فخر الدين عن بعضهم أنه ذهب إلى أن اسم الله تعالى عبراني لا عربي ، ثم ضعفه

rows.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد
rows.claim: Al-Khalil explains that all creation is captivated by God, using a form of the root “to worship.”
rows.anchor: لأن الخلق يألهون إليه بنصب اللام وجرها لغتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further proposal derives Allah from elevation: Arabs called something high lahan and said lahat when the sun rose.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنه مشتق من الارتفاع ، فكانت العرب تقول لكل شيء مرتفع : لاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed form begins as al-ilah; deleting the hamza brings two lams together, which assimilate and are pronounced as one emphatic doubled lam.
rows.anchor: وأصل ذلك الإله ، فحذفت الهمزة التي هي فاء الكلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are intensive forms derived from mercy, with al-Rahman more emphatic; Ibn Jarir's discussion suggests agreement.
rows.anchor: اسمان مشتقان من الرحمة على وجه المبالغة

rows.speaker: عيسى ابن مريم
rows.claim: A report attributed to Jesus distinguishes Rahman as merciful in this life and the next, and Rahim as merciful in the next life.
rows.anchor: والرحمن رحمن الدنيا والآخرة ، والرحيم رحيم الآخرة

rows.speaker: المبرد وأحمد بن يحيى
rows.claim: Some grammarians claim Rahman is not derived or is Hebrew while Rahim is Arabic; al-Zajjaj rejects this as an objectionable view.
rows.anchor: وقال أحمد بن يحيى : الرحيم عربي ، والرحمن عبراني ، فلهذا جمع بينهما

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi cites the hadith, graded sound by al-Tirmidhi, in which God says He is Rahman and derived the womb's name from His own; he treats it as explicit evidence of derivation.
rows.anchor: أنا الرحمن خلقت الرحم وشققت لها اسمًا من اسمي

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi says Arabs denied the name Rahman through ignorance of God and what is due to Him.
rows.anchor: وإنكار العرب لاسم الرحمن لجهلهم بالله وبما وجب له

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayd treats Rahman and Rahim as synonymous, like two parallel forms; others distinguish the intensive faʿlan form from faʿil.
rows.anchor: هما بمعنى واحد كندمان ونديم قاله أبو عبيد

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abu ʿAli al-Farisi says Rahman encompasses every kind of mercy and is exclusive to God, while Rahim describes His mercy toward believers.
rows.anchor: الرحمن : اسم عام في جميع أنواع الرحمة يختص به الله تعالى ، والرحيم إنما هو من جهة المؤمنين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas calls the two names tender and says one is more tender—that is, more merciful—than the other.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس : هما اسمان رقيقان ، أحدهما أرق من الآخر

rows.speaker: ابن المبارك
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mubarak says Rahman gives when asked, while Rahim becomes angry if not asked, linking the distinction to the hadith that God is angered by one who does not supplicate.
rows.anchor: الرحمن إذا سئل أعطى ، والرحيم إذا لم يسأل يغضب

rows.speaker: العرزمي
rows.claim: Al-ʿArzami says Rahman covers all creation, while Rahim specifically describes mercy to believers.
rows.anchor: الرحمن لجميع الخلق ، الرحيم ، قال : بالمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This distinction is supported by verses that name Rahman at God's establishing the Throne and Rahim for believers, although a traditional supplication calls Him Rahman and Rahim of both worlds.
rows.anchor: فدل على أن الرحمن أشد مبالغة في الرحمة لعمومها في الدارين لجميع خلقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahman is a name specific to God; Musaylima's self-title Rahman of Yamama became a byword for lying.
rows.anchor: واسمه تعالى الرحمن خاص به لم يسم به غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Rahim must intensify Rahman because it follows it is mistaken: the second word is another adjective, not emphatic repetition.
rows.anchor: وإنما هو من باب النعت [ بعد النعت ]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The naming sequence moves from the unique name Allah, to the exclusive Rahman, to Rahim, which also describes the Prophet and human beings; naming starts with the most honored and specific names.
rows.anchor: فلهذا بدأ باسم الله ، ووصفه بالرحمن ؛ لأنه أخص وأعرف من الرحيم

rows.speaker: عطاء الخراساني
rows.claim: ʿAta al-Khurasani explains that Rahim follows Rahman to prevent anyone claiming the exclusive title Rahman, since only God is described as both.
rows.anchor: جيء بلفظ الرحيم ليقطع التوهم بذلك ، فإنه لا يوصف بالرحمن الرحيم إلا الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh's denial of Rahman at Hudaybiyya and in 25:60 was stubbornness: pre-Islamic poems already used Rahman for God.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن إنكارهم هذا إنما هو جحود وعناد وتعنت في كفرهم

rows.speaker: سلامة بن جندب
rows.claim: Salama ibn Jundub's pre-Islamic verse calls God Rahman, showing the name was already known among Arabs.
rows.anchor: وما يشأ الرحمن يعقد ويطلق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas calls Rahman an intensive Arabic form of mercy and glosses the two names as gentle to whom God wills mercy and severe toward whom He wills to chastise.
rows.anchor: عن الضحاك ،   عن عبد الله بن عباس ،   قال : الرحمن : الفعلان من الرحمة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says Rahman is a protected name that people cannot assume for themselves.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن ، قال : الرحمن اسم ممنوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umm Salama's report says the Prophet paused between the basmala, al-Hamd, Rahman al-Rahim, and Malik yawm al-din; some Kufans pause at the basmala while most connect it to al-Hamd.
rows.anchor: حديث أم سلمة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يقطع قرآنه حرفًا حرفًا

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi says some Arabs connect the basmala to al-Hamd by transferring the vowel of the connecting hamza to the mīm; Ibn ʿAtiyya says he knew of no transmitted canonical reading for it.
rows.anchor: وحكى الكسائي عن بعض العرب أنها تقرأ بفتح الميم وصلة الهمزة
